blocks.text: An IP address is a unique number assigned to a device. IP stands for Internet Protocol. It helps identify devices on a network. Data uses IP addresses to find its destination. Every network device must have an IP address. Communication is not possible without it.

IPv4 is an older version of IP addressing. It uses 32-bit numeric addresses. IPv4 has a limited number of addresses. IPv6 is the newer version with 128-bit addresses. IPv6 provides more address space. It supports modern Internet needs.
IPv4 has 4 numbers, each 0–255, separated by dots.

blocks.caption: Breakdown of IPv4
rows: Identifies your local network, like “Gulshan Block Street 3”
Identifies your specific device on that network, like “House #10”

blocks.text: IPv6 has 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits, separated by colons.

blocks.caption: Breakdown of IPv6
rows: Your local network inside the ISP, like “Gulshan area”

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text:
• IPv6 addresses comprise: 2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸ total addresses.
• IPv6 will never run out; it is an astronomically massive number.

Subnetting divides a network into smaller parts. Each part is called a subnet (as shown in Figure 1.15). It reduces network traffic. Subnetting improves performance. It increases security. Large networks use subnetting for management.

blocks.alt: The network 192.168.1.0/24 at the top splits by dashed lines into Subnet 1 (192.168.1.0/25), holding a desktop computer, a network device and a laptop, and Subnet 2 (192.168.1.128/25), holding a mobile phone and a printer.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.15: Subnetting Example (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.15).

blocks.text: NAT stands for Network Address Translation. It allows many devices to share one public IP address. NAT is performed by routers. It hides private IP addresses. This improves network security. NAT is commonly used in networks.
